newsitem.title: VIETNAM: Economic habits die hard in Vietnam's tea industry.
newsitem.headline: Economic habits die hard in Vietnam's tea industry.

text.p: The director of Song Cau Tea Company stands proudly on the clean-swept floor of his processing plant and points to a bank of modern machinery.
"In the old days, we used to use equipment from the USSR," says Tran Lien with a raucous laugh as he heads off to put the kettle on for yet another cup of green tea.
Indeed, times have changed at the Hoa Trung tea plantations in the hills of northern Vietnam, a showcase for the modern, commercial face of state-owned Vietnam Tea Corp (Vinatea).
One of Vinatea's 25 subsidiaries, Song Cau is a cooperation project with Nissho Iwai Corp of Japan, which provided the technical know-how and equipment.
In return, the company makes use of a cheap local workforce to pick and process connoisseur green tea that would suit even the most refined Tokyo palate -- and then ships it, at a discount, to Japan.

In a country where setting up a joint venture with a foreign company can be a nightmare of red tape and expense, Vinatea reckons cooperation projects are a smart idea. It already has a similar deal with a Taiwanese firm and is looking to set up more.
Vietnam exported 16,000-17,000 tonnes of its 38,000-tonne crop last year, mostly to the Middle East and the former Soviet bloc, earning between $26 and $27 million.
That is about seventeen times less than it makes out of selling coffee abroad, but still a tidy sum for one of the poorest countries in the world.

Song Cau is no giant. It grows tea on 400 ha (988 acres), which yields about 400 tonnes of dried tea leaves a year. With a sale price of around $3 per kg (2.2 lbs), the company's turnover comes to little more than $1 million a year.
This year it is aiming to step up production to 450 tonnes by ploughing money into organic fertilisers, peg its selling price higher and go from break-even to a profit of $20,000-30,000.

The bottom line has become increasingly important for Vietnam's state-owned companies, which now face competition from a private sector that has grown up out of the communist government's 10-year-old drive to embrace market principles.
The number of state-owned firms has been halved to some 6,250 companies in an effort to cut away dead wood, but thousands are still in poor health.

Nevertheless, the government is determined to make the state sector play a leading role in the economy. It has ruled out privatisation, despite ambitions to set up a stock market, and even its more modest plan for partial privatisation, or "equitisation", is moving at a glacial pace.

As Lien strides around the plantation in sandals and an open-neck shirt, it's hard to imagine him poring over spread sheets and cash-flow charts. Corporate vital statistics seem of less interest to him than the fact that his 700 workers have been allotted 1,600 ha acres (3,952 acres) to grow tea or other crops for themselves.
Back at Vinatea's headquarters in Hanoi, the same thinking holds sway.

"When we talk about profit, we should also talk about the environment and employment," says General Director Nguyen Kim Phong. "Our main targets are to create more jobs and ensure reforestation. Everything should be for the people first."

Phong says he has no idea when Vinatea will be equitised and, when asked how much profit it makes on annual turnover of $25.62 million, he simply explains that the company spends money on building roads and other infrastructure in and around tea farms.
Vinatea's share of nationwide output is slightly more than a third, but its share of the total area under tea cultivation -- 70,000 ha (172,970 acres) -- is just 10 percent.
"That's the advantage of being a state firm," says Phong with a grin. "We have better productivity and better facilities."
